text:
Recent work distinguishes useful temporal modeling from excessive recency dependence. [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) introduces a recency-bias metric and reports improved accuracy after mitigating excessive emphasis on recent interactions. [CETRec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03047) distinguishes absolute order—how recently an interaction occurred—from relative order between interactions, using counterfactual tuning for LLM recommenders. These motivate separate recency and ordering probes; their findings do not establish that greater sensitivity is always desirable.

Strong simple baselines matter. [Petrov et al. (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19833) compare Transformers with recency-weighted pairwise probes, SeqRules and PCTM. At least one probe outperforms their eSASRec reproduction on three Amazon datasets, while results differ elsewhere. Recommendation changes after history perturbation can therefore reflect pairwise associations and recency weighting without demonstrating higher-order sequence reasoning.

Practical synthesis: evaluate the trained model with dropout disabled; mask equal numbers of recent, older, and randomly selected interactions; shuffle nonpadding items while preserving the item multiset; separately preserve the final item to isolate earlier ordering. Remove duplicate occurrences while retaining one occurrence, where duplicates exist; alternatively remove clusters defined using available titles/descriptions to probe repeated narrow interests. Compare against random removals matched for count, item popularity, and position where applicable. Keep candidate sets fixed; report target-rank changes, top-10 overlap, and paired validation HR@10 differences, broken down by category and history length. Preserve padding conventions and distinguish masking from deletion/reindexing. These are proposed diagnostics: sensitivity measures model dependence, while validation changes assess predictive usefulness. Neither alone identifies true preference drift or causal correctness.
